description: We are a diverse team with different backgrounds and interests, united by curiosity about space technology and exploration. We saw this challenge as a chance to combine our varied skills—research, design, coding—toward building something meaningful. Our focus is creating something educational and interactive that genuinely engages people, rather than simply presenting information.
summary: Stellar Scripts is a narrated, interactive book that tells the stories of six machines NASA left behind on Mars, on the Moon and in deep space. Readers step into a depth-layered virtual study, open a chapter and press Narrate: the page turns, the spoken words light up and original diagrams draw themselves in sync with the audio, beside real NASA photographs. The six machines are Spirit, Opportunity, Pioneer 10, Pioneer 11, Ingenuity and Surveyor 3. A built-in chatbot, the Archive, answers readers' questions using only the verified, NASA-sourced fact sheet for that chapter, and says so when it does not know. We built it to make real mission history memorable for school-age students and casual space fans, communicating the value of NASA's open mission data through storytelling. Abandoned, but not forgotten.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Stellar Scripts is a narrated, interactive book about six machines NASA left behind: Spirit, Opportunity, Pioneer 10, Pioneer 11, Ingenuity and Surveyor 3. Readers enter a layered virtual study, open one of four chapters and press Narrate. An AI-generated voice tells a roughly 90-second story, and the audio clock drives everything on screen: the book turns to the next page at the right moment, the spoken sentence is highlighted word by word, and original diagrams animate as they are mentioned (for example, a counter ticks to twenty-eight airbag bounces, and a power gauge rises from 60 to 93 percent). Real NASA photographs and video sit beside the diagrams with their credit lines. There are 29 pages in total. Each pairs one idea with one visual and one key number: a hook, what the machine was, the challenge it faced, its discovery and its legacy. Without narration, every page still reads as a finished static page.

Each chapter also has "Ask the Archive", a chatbot (Google Gemini) that receives only that chapter's verified fact sheet. It answers only from those facts, keeps twin machines apart, never presents a source-conflicting figure as settled, never says anything on the fact sheet's "must not claim" list, and says it has no verified information instead of guessing. Answers are written for a 10 to 14 year old.

BENEFITS

Readers learn why each machine was built, what it faced and what it discovered, in about 90 seconds a chapter, without reading dense mission pages. Narration, highlighting and diagrams arrive together, so the story is easy to follow. It is free, runs in a browser and needs nothing to install. The chatbot lets curious readers go deeper without leaving verified facts.

INTENDED IMPACT

We want school-age students and casual space fans to care about NASA's retired hardware and see what open mission data makes possible. A chapter works as a short classroom story. The approach is reusable: a new machine needs a script, an audio file, a page plan and diagrams, and the page timing is generated automatically.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES AND SOFTWARE

HTML, CSS and JavaScript (canvas scenes, CSS 3D page turns, original SVG diagrams); React and Babel loaded in the browser; a Node.js server with one chat endpoint; Google Gemini API for the chatbot; ElevenLabs text-to-speech for narration; PocketSphinx for offline narration timing; Google Fonts; Vercel for hosting; GitHub for the source code. No special hardware is needed.

NASA data: all facts, photographs and video come from NASA mission pages, press releases, archives and the Photojournal, including the resources the challenge page lists. Each source is linked in the NASA Data field. The 14 photographs and video clips are shown with NASA's credit lines, and a credits page lists each one and its source.

Use of SI: Claude (Anthropic) helped organise the source material into fact sheets, draft the narration scripts, and write much of the website code and the original SVG diagrams. Our team reviewed and tested them. The narration is AI-generated (ElevenLabs), and the chatbot is powered by Google Gemini, limited to our fact sheets. The diagrams are SI-assisted original illustrations and are labelled as such. All photographs and video are authentic NASA media.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

Instead of a slideshow or a fact list, we built a book that performs its own story. The audio clock turns the pages, lights up the words and draws the diagrams, and the study around it shifts in layers with the cursor. The story is told through the machines' challenges and discoveries, not as a list of dates. The chatbot is a character in the archive: a careful librarian that would rather say "I don't have verified information" than guess.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Scientific accuracy came first. Each chapter has a fact sheet listing its sources, documented source conflicts, known gaps and a "must not claim" list. Narration and callouts use numbers from those sheets, and schematic diagrams are labelled "not to scale". Images whose credit we could not confirm, or that carry private copyright, were left out or flagged. We designed for the audience: short pages, one idea at a time, and plain language. The 3D page turn is a CSS effect that is turned off on small screens and when reduced motion is requested, and every page works as static text. We kept it to a polished, working prototype that tells six stories well, rather than adding more features.
